name: Daria Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My brother Lukas and I run a wedding and events band called The Silver Lanterns. I sing and play rhythm guitar, he plays keys and does the sound. We play about eighty events a year, mostly weddings, some company parties. During the week I do the bookings and I record voice jingles for local radio adverts at a studio across town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up running a band with your brother?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our dad had a wedding band in the nineties, and we grew up hauling his speakers. When he retired, Lukas and I took over the name and the van. Our dad still turns up at our bigger weddings and tells the bride he taught us everything, which is mostly true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it. People will always want a real band at their wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the same. I already use a chatbot sometimes to draft quotes for couples, and that's handy. The jingle studio might use a few AI voices for cheap spots, but nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the band going, keep the bookings full. Maybe buy a new PA system with Lukas, because the old one's on its last legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a new PA cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twelve thousand, split between us. We've saved for it. A new PA system is the best thing we could buy for the band, because a wedding with bad sound is a wedding people remember for the wrong reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our dad's health. He had a small heart scare in the spring. Lukas and I keep an eye on him.

I'd tell people to just **get on with it**, not worry.
think: I already use a **chatbot** sometimes for quotes, and that's handy.
The jingle studio might use **AI voices** for cheap spots, nothing big.
do: Buy a **new PA system** with Lukas, about twelve thousand split between them.

steps.text: Keep The Silver Lanterns booked for about eighty events a year
Buy a new PA system with Lukas for about twelve thousand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and you adapt or you don't. I'm not one for complaining. People who work hard will find their way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the jingle work goes. That's maybe a fifth of my income. Booking work could be done by AI too, but I'd rather do it myself because couples like talking to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the jingles and push harder on band bookings, maybe ninety events a year. I'd use AI for quotes and scheduling more, once I see it really works. And I'd keep our prices steady to stay competitive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A fifth is a lot, but not the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you replace that fifth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More company parties, maybe Christmas season bookings. Losing the jingle work means ten more weddings a year, and my voice can take ten more weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lukas worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than me. He does the sound and keys, and nobody's replacing him at a live gig soon.

I'd say people who **work hard** will find their way.
think: The **jingle work** goes, maybe a fifth of my income.
I'd keep **booking work** myself because couples like talking to me.
do: Drop jingles and push the band to **ninety events** a year.
Use **AI for quotes** and scheduling once she sees it work.
feel: **Uneasy**: losing a fifth is a lot but not the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast for anyone to keep up, but families and businesses should look after their own first. I wouldn't wait for government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about couples' budgets. If people lose jobs in 2028, weddings get smaller and cheaper, maybe a playlist instead of a band. Robots playing weddings by 2031 seems silly, but who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut our prices a little to keep bookings. I'd keep the PA purchase on hold. And I'd talk to Lukas about taking on corporate events, because companies with money will still throw parties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Bookings are our whole income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider changing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The band is the family business. The Silver Lanterns (her band) has been in my family for thirty years, and I'm not giving up the band because of a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'll manage, like he did in the hard years. He'd tell us to keep our prices fair and our sound good.

fieldNote: Daria's risk is **clients' incomes**, not her craft.
She'd hold to the **family business**, and won't change jobs.
Her father's **hard years** are her model.

steps.text: Lower wedding prices slightly to keep the calendar full
Postpone the twelve-thousand PA system purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, and people should get on with it rather than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about wedding budgets around 2031. But five years means we can build up corporate work and savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the PA now, while times are good, and save hard after that. I'd build a corporate client list with Lukas. And I'd learn AI for bookings, because it'd save me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. We'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the PA now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if bookings drop later, we won't want to spend twelve thousand. Buying the PA system before the hard years is what my dad would call fixing the roof while the sun shines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save toward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cushion for the band, a year of costs. And maybe my own flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should be sensible about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm thirty-seven. The band would probably still be going, maybe with Lukas's kids hauling the speakers like we did. Weddings will still need music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the band growing. Use AI for the admin. Maybe buy my own flat in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own flat. Near your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, same street if I can. I'd buy a flat on my parents' street so I can look after my dad and still be home in time for the Saturday load-in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because couples would cut wedding budgets before we could adjust. What would help is businesses keeping people in work, and families sticking together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. A lot of musicians work with family, and that's what holds us together when times get hard.

headlineQuote: Our dad still turns up at our bigger weddings and tells the bride he taught us everything, which is mostly true.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old** singer and guitarist who co-runs a family wedding band with her brother.
She's **traditional**, believes in hard work, and uses AI only now and then.
Her **jingle work** goes early, but she trusts live weddings to last.
Her risk is **clients' budgets** in fast AGI.
**Family** shapes everything: her dad's health, the band's history, living nearby.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because wedding budgets would fall before she could adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Businesses** keeping people in work, and families sticking together.
